title: The second arrow
hook: pain is one arrow; the distress we add is a second (SN 36.6)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was vedana, feeling tone. Your line: pleasant, painful, neither. Did you catch the feeling before you reached for your phone? Day two hundred fifty-seven.

You stub your toe on the bed frame at night. There's the pain, sharp and real. And then, within a second: who put this bed here, why am I so clumsy, this always happens to me, now I'll never get back to sleep. The toe hurt for thirty seconds. The rest of it went on for twenty minutes. The Buddha has a short teaching about exactly this, and it's one of the most useful ideas in the whole tradition. Today: the second arrow.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE AT NIGHT.` → `THIRTY SECONDS OF PAIN.` → `TWENTY MINUTES OF THE REST.`

segments.voice: The teaching is in the Connected Discourses, a sutta called the Arrow. The Buddha asks his monks a question. When an ordinary person and a well-trained disciple both feel pain, what's the difference? Then he answers with an image. An untrained person, touched by a painful feeling, worries, grieves, laments, beats their chest and becomes distraught. It's as if they were struck by an arrow, and then struck by a second arrow right after. They feel two pains: one in the body, one in the mind. The well-trained disciple, touched by the same painful feeling, doesn't add the worry and the lament. They are struck by one arrow, and not by a second. They feel one pain, the bodily one, and not the other. Notice what the Buddha doesn't say. He doesn't say the trained person feels no pain. The first arrow lands on everyone, including, in the texts, the Buddha himself, who had backaches and grew old. The teaching is only about the second arrow, the one we fire at ourselves. And he adds something sharp. When pain comes, the untrained person often runs toward sensual pleasure to escape it, because they know no other way out. That's a third trap, hidden inside the second. This links straight back to yesterday. Pain is a feeling, vedana. The second arrow is what we do next. If you can see the feeling as just a feeling, you've stopped the second arrow before it leaves the bow.
screen: `THE ARROW SUTTA.` · `STRUCK BY ONE, THEN BY A SECOND.` · `THE FIRST ARROW LANDS ON EVERYONE.` · `THE SECOND IS THE ONE WE FIRE.` · then, large: `ONE ARROW, NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and find some small discomfort: a stiff knee, an itch, a tight shoulder, or a worry you've been carrying. Feel the first arrow: just the raw sensation, or the plain fact. Then watch for the second arrow: the story, the complaint, the why me. When you notice it, name it quietly: second arrow. Then return to the first, and let it be only what it is. The bell holds the time.
The second arrow. Pain is the first arrow, and it lands on everyone. The distress we add on top is the second, and we fire it ourselves.
Your line: one arrow, not two. Today, when something goes wrong, catch one second arrow before it lands, and say to yourself: one arrow, not two. Day two hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers of many schools use the two arrows image from the Sallatha Sutta, and it is widely used in pain care and mindfulness courses to separate physical pain from the distress added to it.

match.prompt: match each piece of the arrow teaching.
pairs: worry, grief and lament we add
the trap hidden in the second

myth: the teaching says a trained person feels no pain
the first arrow lands on everyone; the teaching is about the second.
the Buddha himself is said to have had physical pain
the texts mention his backaches and old age.
the second arrow is the distress we add on top
worry, grieving, lamenting: a second pain in the mind.

fork.setup: you're one of the Buddha's monks, and he asks: when an ordinary person and a trained disciple both feel pain, what's the difference?
options: the trained disciple feels no pain at all.
the trained disciple feels the body's pain but doesn't add a second pain of distress.
fork.reveal: both are struck by the first arrow. only the untrained person is struck by the second.

original.note: Pali salla: an arrow or dart; the sutta's name is Sallatha, the arrow.

trapdoor: what you thought: the second arrow means a second bad thing happening.
what it means: the distress we add to pain: the story, the worry, the lament.
what a scholar hears: SN 36.6 adds that the untrained person, not knowing any escape from pain except sensual pleasure, is drawn to it, so the latent tendency to lust also grows.

notes: SN 36.6 is paraphrased; no public-domain translation on the approved list was used (the Pali Text Society's Kindred Sayings vol. 4 is by Woodward, not on the list).
The Buddha's backaches (e.g. DN 33, MN 53) and old age (SN 48.41): confirm the references.
Mention of pain-care and mindfulness courses in howItsDone is a general characterization.
